items.creator: elemental.math
items.caption:
Can one line of math build an entire 3D world? This is the Mandelbulb, and it comes from z ↦ z⁸ + c.

In 2D, the Mandelbrot set repeats z ↦ z² + c: pick a point c, start at zero, square, add c, repeat. If it never escapes past |z| = 2, the point is black. Squaring a complex number squares its length and doubles its angle.

There is no such multiplication for points in 3D. William Rowan Hamilton tried for years; in an 1865 letter he remembers his sons asking every morning, "Well, Papa, can you multiply triplets?" and his answer, "No, I can only add and subtract them." Daniel White's 2007 idea was to copy the geometry in spherical coordinates, and Paul Nylander raised it to the 8th power: r ↦ r⁸, θ ↦ 8θ, φ ↦ 8φ, then add c.

To draw it, every pixel shoots a ray. The formula gives a distance the ray can safely jump, d = ½ · r · log r / dr, and the ray jumps that far and asks again. The ray in the video needed 13 jumps (1.507, 0.219, 0.090 … 0.0009).

One frame of this video, counted pixel by pixel: 8,294,400 rays, 102,780,876 jumps and 307,247,022 turns of the formula (1080 × 1920, 4 rays per pixel, 15 iterations).

The formula, the distance estimate and the ray-marching loop are ported line by line from Mandelbulber's source (GPL-3.0, commit 109fd69): github.com/buddhi1980/mandelbulber2
Hamilton's letter (5 Aug 1865): maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Hamilton/Letters/BroomeBridge.html
Daniel White on the Mandelbulb: skytopia.com/project/fractal/mandelbulb.html

items.caption:
In case you missed it, there’s been turmoil in AI stocks, sparked by concern over Coreweave’s debt. Here’s exactly what you need to know about the neoclouds.

A few things I couldn’t fit in the video time limit of 3 min: 

1. The advance rate, meaning how much neoclouds can borrow relative to the amount of money they need to spend on Capex (to buy chips and equipment) can get QUITE high, in some cases 90-95%+ depending on the credit of the “off-taker”, so from Meta for example. 

2. Asset backed financing and project financing (one of the groups I worked in at Morgan Stanley) isn’t new. What is unique about these GPU backed financings are the much shorter contract length; in the power world you often see power purchase agreements of 15-20 years and assets that have a much longer useful life (think a gas turbine). In a power deal, the debt is shorter than the PPA, and the PPA is shorter than the asset’s life, which leaves a long tail. Here the loan, the contract, and the asset useful life are much closer in length, so there is a shorter tail behind the debt. 

Now in fairness to the neoclouds, after the off-taker's contracts end the same GPUs can be rented on an hourly basis at higher rates (at least right now) because demand for compute is so high.

While Coreweave does have other types of debt, this structure accounts for over half and funded much of its massive growth over the past few years. They also have a decent amount of convertible debt, which is typically utilized by higher risk companies. 

A huge reason for the stock sell off though was the corporate debt yields blew out to 15% (tweeted about by Chamath Palihapitiya to which Elon responded “yikes”), which spooked the market.

3. And finally what surprised me was the fact that on the other side, so if you look at an Anthropic’s balance sheet, “take or pay” agreements to buy the compute do not show up as a liability on the balance sheet, rather just shown as a footnote!!While this is consistent with accounting rules, it’s surprising.

ln + vpype — turning 3D scenes into lines for drawing.

① Build a 3D scene → ② remove hidden lines → ③ export vector paths → ④ arrange the drawing order.

ln removes lines hidden by the geometry. vpype joins and reorders the paths for pen plotting.

These scenes use ln's original examples with added camera motion. In this example, vpype linemerge + linesort reduced pen-up travel by 86% (105,271 → 14,926 px). This measures distance, not the time of a real pen plotter.

Which scene would you turn into a print, an animation, or a pen plot?

The cover is an AI-generated illustration based on the line drawings.

① 3D 장면 만들기 → ② 가려진 선 지우기 → ③ 벡터 경로로 내보내기 → ④ 그리는 순서 정리하기.

items.creator: ryanlpeterman
items.caption:
The only unbreakable law in software engineering

Casey Muratori (Video Game Dev & Creator): What is the only unbreakable law in software engineering? The only thing I've seen that feels like a real law to me is the thing I cover in this lecture, which is Conway's law.

And it is that if you would like to organize a series, like a set of people to work on something, or in the modern parlance, let's say agents, if you need to partition a problem into a set of workers in this way where the communication between those workers is slower than their own internal computation ability, when you start to tackle a problem, in order to get the benefits of that parallelization, you will have to make decisions about who is working on what.

Once you've made that decision, you have now locked in the fact that that the iteration on the design will be slower across that boundary than it is interior to either of the two parts. One way the rule is pithily stated is products look like the org chart, right?

But that's not exactly what it says. But that's a downstream consequence and boy do you ever see it in the real world.

items.creator: techvrix
items.caption:
This is how AI actually learns. 🧠📉

Backpropagation can be understood by imagining a neural network’s total error as a point on a huge, high-dimensional loss surface, where every direction represents a different model parameter.

Each parameter influences the model’s overall loss, and the gradient combines all of those partial derivatives to show how the loss changes with respect to every parameter.

Using the chain rule, backpropagation efficiently calculates this gradient across the entire network.

The negative gradient points in the direction of steepest descent. You can think of it like rolling a ball downhill, where each step moves the model toward a region with lower loss.

The network repeats this process over and over, adjusting its parameters to gradually reduce error and improve its predictions.

That simple idea, calculate the gradient, move downhill, and repeat, is one of the fundamental mechanisms behind how modern neural networks learn.

Credit: Welch Labs

Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI just launched Grok Bot, but the most interesting part isn’t simply that it can create AI workers.

Each user gets a dedicated cloud computer shared across their Grok Bots. Those Bots can have different jobs, pass work between each other, create new long-lived Bots, and even run on different underlying models over time.

That leads to a much bigger idea: your future “job” may not be one AI model or one agent. It could be a persistent cloud computer that accumulates tools, context, responsibilities, and increasingly capable AI workers.

That’s my interpretation, not an xAI claim, but Grok Bot gives us a fascinating look at what that architecture could become.

AI-designed viruses sound terrifying, but these were bacteriophages, meaning viruses that infect bacteria.

A phage is just short for bacteriophage. A genome is the complete set of genetic instructions inside an organism or virus. A mosaic descendant is a later virus whose genome contains pieces inherited from multiple parent phages after recombination.

Researchers used AI to design new phage genomes, tested them in the lab, and found viable designs. Some later recombined into mosaic descendants during experiments. We are now seeing specialized AI models being used to build complex, interrelated systems!

The cinematic visuals in this video were made with SeeDance 2.5 to explore a more unusual use case for AI video generation. They are illustrative entertainment, not scientifically exact renderings, and should not be treated as factual depictions of molecular structures or experimental events.

Melvin Conway sent this to Harvard Business Review in 1967 and they rejected it for not proving its thesis. Datamation ran it a year later. The claim: any organisation that designs a system produces a design that copies that organisation’s own communication structure. Four teams building a compiler ship a compiler with four parts.
The elaboration the video does not make: engineers now use this deliberately and call it the reverse Conway manoeuvre. Decide the architecture you want first, then arrange the teams to match, because the mirroring happens either way and the only real choice is whether it happens on purpose.
Your customers are holding a physical copy of your org chart, and they experience it as friction. Which handoff in your product is really two teams that barely speak?

What to do about it, written out properly: shakibhammad.com/library/conway

items.creator: algomasterio
items.caption:
10 Must-Know Time Complexity Patterns for Interviews

1. 𝐇𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐮𝐩 - 𝐎(1) 𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞
A lookup usually takes constant time, regardless of input size. In the worst case, it can degrade to O(n).

2. 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 - 𝐎(𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐧)
The input size is divided by a constant factor in every step, such as in binary search.

3. 𝐒𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 - 𝐎(𝐧)
Each element is processed once.

4. 𝐒𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬 - 𝐎(𝐧 + 𝐦)
You iterate over two separate inputs one after another, not with one loop nested inside the other.

5. 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 + 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐒𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 - 𝐎(𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐧)
A loop runs n times, and each iteration performs O(log n) work.

6. 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞 & 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐫 - 𝐎(𝐧 𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐧)
The problem is divided across roughly log n levels, with O(n) total work at each level. Merge sort is a common example.

7. 𝐍𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩𝐬 - 𝐎(𝐧²)
For every element, you iterate over all elements again.

8. 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩 - 𝐎(𝐧²)
The inner loop performs fewer iterations each time, but the total is still roughly n(n − 1) / 2, which is quadratic.

9. 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 - 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐞
When each recursive call creates multiple new calls, the work can grow exponentially.

10. 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 - 𝐎(𝐧!)
There are n! possible orderings, and producing or copying each complete permutation can take O(n) time.
